description.value: The study examined whether cerebellar activity during visual motion perception reflects sustained covert attention to motion or the detection and discrimination of motion under high perceptual uncertainty.

spans.text: Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to determine the degree to which cerebellar involvement in visual motion perception can be explained by a role in sustained attentive tracking of moving stimuli in contrast to a role in visual motion discrimination.

design.value: An event-related fMRI study manipulated attention by directing participants covertly to motion or a fixation spot and manipulated perceptual uncertainty by varying motion coherence.

spans.text: While holding the visual displays constant, we manipulated attention by having participants attend covertly to a field of random-dot motion or a colored spot at fixation. Perceptual uncertainty was manipulated by varying the percentage of signal dots contained within the random-dot arrays.
While holding the visual displays constant, we manipulated attention by having participants attend covertly to a field of random-dot motion or a colored spot at fixation.
The participants' task was to attend covertly to the moving dots and monitor for periods of motion coherence, or to attend to the central spot and monitor for color changes.

The aim of this study was to determine the degree to which cerebellar activity during visual motion perception can be explained by a role in aiding attentive tracking of visual motion, in contrast to a role in facilitating visual motion discrimination under levels of high perceptual uncertainty.
Three levels of motion coherence (0, 15, and 30 %; see Animations 1-3 in Supplemental Material) were presented.

model_settings.value: Boxcar functions modeled the exact duration of each stimulation period; high-pass filtering cutoff was 128 s; respiratory and cardiac noise models and six head-motion regressors were included.

spans.text: We modeled the exact duration of each individual stimulation period (i.e. 4.7, 8.5, 11.2, or 16 s) in SPM so that the height and duration of the corresponding HRFs were scaled accordingly for every trial.

To account for physiological noise, we used the Physiological Log Extraction for Modeling toolbox [21] to compute models of respiratory and cardiac noise, which were included in the general linear model as regressors.
We further included the six head motion regressors into the model (x, y, z, pitch, roll, and yaw) to account for movement artifacts.
The relevant conditions were contrasted using t-statistics, generating the contrast images for second level evaluation.

interpretations.value: the cerebellum facilitates the detection and discrimination of moving objects under conditions of high perceptual uncertainty

spans.text: Our results therefore support the notion that the cerebellum facilitates the detection and discrimination of moving objects under conditions of high perceptual uncertainty [4, 9], but are inconsistent with the idea that the cerebellum is crucial for sustained attentive tracking of salient motion stimuli [10-13].

First, to test the degree to which the cerebellum is involved in sustained attentive tracking of moving objects we compared the level of BOLD signal associated with attention to a salient supra-threshold motion signal (i.e., no perceptual uncertainty) with the corresponding color-control condition [attend motion (30 %)>attend color (30 %)].

We also performed exploratory whole-brain analyses using the comparison of the condition requiring attention to a salient suprathreshold motion signal with the corresponding color-control condition [attend motion (30 %)>attend color (30 %)].
